title: Largest Merge Of Two Strings
statement:
You are given two strings `word1` and `word2`. Build a string `merge`, which starts empty, by repeating one move until both words are used up: pick either word that still has characters, cut off its first character, and add that character to the end of `merge`.

Return the lexicographically largest `merge` that some sequence of moves can produce. Every possible `merge` has the same length, and of two such strings the larger one is the one with the later letter of the alphabet at the first index where they differ.
constraints: word1 and word2 contain only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Lexicographic order is decided by the first difference, so the first character of `merge` should be as large as possible, then the second, and so on. When the two fronts differ, taking the larger letter is clearly right. The hard case is a tie: with `word1 = "ab"` and `word2 = "ac"` both start with `a`, but taking from `word2` first brings its `c` forward sooner. The rule that settles every case at once: take from the word whose **whole remaining suffix** is larger. That suffix is exactly what that word could still contribute next, so it wins any tie for the longest time. Trying both choices at every step (the brute force) explores exponentially many merges.

## Approach

1. Keep a pointer `i` into `word1` and `j` into `word2`, and collect characters in `merge`.
2. While either word has characters left, compare `word1.slice(i)` with `word2.slice(j)`.
3. If `word1`'s suffix is larger, append `word1[i]` and advance `i`; otherwise append `word2[j]` and advance `j`.
4. Join and return `merge`.

An empty suffix is smaller than any non-empty one, so once a word runs out the other is copied to the end automatically.

## Example 1, step by step

`word1 = "cabaa"`, `word2 = "bcaaa"`. `"cabaa" > "bcaaa"`, take `c`. `"abaa" < "bcaaa"`, take `b`. `"abaa" < "caaa"`, take `c`. `"abaa" > "aaa"`, take `a`. `"baa" > "aaa"`, take `b`. Then `"aa" < "aaa"` (a prefix is smaller), so the remaining five `a`s follow, giving `"cbcabaaaaa"`.

## Complexity

- Time: O((m + n)²) in the worst case: m + n steps, each comparing suffixes that may share a long prefix.
- Space: O(m + n) for the result.

## Pitfalls

- Comparing only `word1[i]` and `word2[j]` fails on ties such as `"ab"` and `"ac"`.
- A suffix that is a prefix of the other is the smaller one: `"aa" < "aaa"`, so take from the longer run of the same letter.
- When the two suffixes are equal, either choice leads to the same merge, so the `else` branch may safely take from `word2`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `i` | index of the next unused character of `word1` |
| `j` | index of the next unused character of `word2` |
| `merge` | the characters chosen so far, in order |

narration.2: i points at the first character word1 has not given up yet.
narration.3: j does the same for word2.
narration.4: merge collects the chosen characters in order.
narration.5: Keep going until both words are used up.
narration.6: Take from the word whose remaining suffix is larger; this also settles ties between equal front letters.
narration.7: word1 wins: append its front character...
narration.10: Otherwise word2's suffix is at least as large: append its front character...
narration.14: Glue the chosen characters into the answer.
